e.t: Abidan is a proper name referring to a person. It is rendered as “Abidan” and is also associated with the form “Avithan.” In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs five times, all in the book of Numbers. The name appears in lists and records concerning Israel’s tribes and leaders, but the name itself identifies the person rather than describing a quality, action, or role. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and account.

This LXX adjective describes someone or something that remains unswerving and undeterred rather than being turned aside. It expresses steadfast direction, purpose, or resolve in the face of opposition or pressure. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament translation, in 3 Maccabees 3:3. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is firm persistence without deviation.

Aziph, also rendered Azif, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a person or place by name rather than expressing an action, quality, or idea. This name occurs twice in the LXX, both times in Joshua, at Joshua 11:1 and Joshua 12:20. Without the surrounding verse text, the name’s specific referent cannot be described further here; its basic meaning is the proper designation Aziph or Azif.

This word is a proper name meaning “Ailameitēs” or “Elamitis.” It identifies the named subject rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Isaiah 11:11. The available lexical information preserves the name but does not provide the verse’s surrounding wording, so its precise role in that sentence must be determined from the passage itself. Its basic function remains identification.

Akoub, also rendered Akuv, is a proper name used for a person in the Greek Old Testament. It does not describe an action, quality, or general object; it identifies an individual by name. This name appears four times in the Greek Old Testament, in 1 Chronicles, Ezra, and Nehemiah. The available information identifies the name and its occurrences, but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain anything further about the person or the role connected with the name.

“Rekindle” means to kindle something again, restoring a fire or its active strength after it has faded. It is a verb, so it describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In this Greek biblical corpus, it occurs twice, once in Genesis and once in 1 Maccabees. The central idea is renewal: something that had diminished is made burning or active again. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse.

This adjective describes someone as “like an effeminate man.” It is a descriptive term applied to a person, identifying a resemblance or manner rather than naming an action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 19:15. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, the word’s exact force in that passage cannot be stated beyond this basic description. Its central meaning remains a comparison to an effeminate man.

This adjective describes someone or something that has not been defeated or cannot be overcome. It can therefore emphasize steadfastness, resistance, or victory over opposition, depending on the sentence where it appears. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, the word occurs six times, all in the deuterocanonical books of 2, 3, and 4 Maccabees. Its central idea remains the same: being unconquered in fact or unconquerable in strength. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis is on an achieved victory or an enduring quality.

“Opposite” means directly facing or positioned across from something. As an adverb, this word describes how or where an action or position relates to another: it points to being opposite rather than merely nearby or different. In the Greek Septuagint, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 5:16. The exact force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence, which is not included here.

This Greek LXX noun means “breastband” or “girdle,” referring to a band or fastening worn around the body. It names a physical clothing item rather than an action or quality. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX, in Song of Songs 1:13. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning remains a breastband or girdle.

gl: drive from house and home; banish
d: drive from house and home; banish

e.t: This Greek LXX verb means to drive someone from house and home—to banish or force that person away. It describes an action of removing someone from a place or community, rather than merely asking the person to leave. The word appears twice in the Greek Old Testament corpus: once in Proverbs and once in 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and scene, but its central idea remains expulsion from one’s home or established place.

This adjective describes something cut off, abrupt, or sharply ended rather than gradual. It can characterize an action, judgment, movement, or change that happens suddenly or decisively, depending on the sentence. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs five times, all in the book of Wisdom. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what it modifies and the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “light.” As a verb, it expresses an action involving light rather than naming a person, object, or quality. Its exact force in a verse depends on what is being acted upon and the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains the act of lighting. It occurs 22 times in the Greek LXX corpus represented here, including one occurrence in Wisdom.

This word is a proper name: “Armathaim,” also given as “Armathem.” It identifies a named entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or relationship. In the LXX corpus, it occurs 12 times, all in 1 Samuel, so its meaning is chiefly the name itself rather than a broader descriptive idea. The surrounding verse is needed to explain what the named entity is doing or how it relates to the passage.

This verb means “stare”: to look steadily and intently at someone or something. It describes a sustained gaze rather than a brief glance. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 2:26. The word identifies the act of fixing one’s eyes on an object or person, while the surrounding passage determines the specific reason, emotion, or significance of that gaze.

This adjective describes something that looks dry, parched, or squalid in appearance. It can portray a visibly harsh, barren, or neglected condition rather than simply naming an object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times, all within five verses, with four occurrences in 1 Samuel and one in Micah. The precise thing being described depends on the surrounding sentence, but the word consistently directs attention to an outward appearance marked by dryness or unpleasant barrenness.

This word means “thistle,” a prickly plant. It is a noun used to name this kind of vegetation. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in 2 Chronicles 25:18. The word therefore identifies a physical plant rather than an action, quality, or person. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and its comparison or description there.

This verb means “dip”: to place or lower something into a substance. It describes an action performed on an object, rather than a person, place, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 15 times across 15 verses, showing repeated use for this straightforward physical action. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on what is being dipped and what substance is involved.

This noun refers to slander or envy—harmful speech about another person or resentful ill will toward what another has or is. It can name either the damaging expression or the inward attitude behind it, depending on the sentence. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs three times, all in deuterocanonical books. Its basic sense therefore points to a destructive attitude or action that injures another through jealous feeling or harmful speech.

This Greek LXX verb means “neighbour” or “border on”: it describes being next to another person, place, or area, or sharing a boundary with it. As a verb, it expresses adjacency rather than movement toward something. It occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 2 Maccabees 9:25. The precise force in that sentence depends on the surrounding verse text, but its basic idea is closeness or a common border.

Gerara is a proper name for a place, also rendered “Yerara.” It identifies a location rather than describing an action, quality, or person. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs 11 times, appearing mainly in Genesis and once in 1 Chronicles. The name is found in passages such as Genesis 10:19, Genesis 20:1–2, and Genesis 26:1, 6, and 8. Its precise significance in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and narrative.

This verb means “naked,” describing a person who is without clothing. It functions as an action word for being in that condition rather than naming a person, object, or place. In the Greek Old Testament represented here, it occurs once, in Genesis 9:21. The word’s basic meaning is limited and concrete; the surrounding verse is needed to explain the particular situation in which it appears.

Darkōn, also rendered Tharkon, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezra 2:56, identifying a person or family in that passage. The name itself does not provide a further lexical description, so its precise significance depends on the surrounding Ezra context. This Greek LXX name should be kept distinct from similarly rendered names or words in other biblical language traditions.

This verb means “lord of; master of,” describing the act of ruling over or exercising mastery. It presents someone as holding authority over another person or thing, rather than merely possessing it. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 5:28. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central sense is authority expressed through mastery or rule. [p03:word:lxx:L703378:identity] [p03:word:lxx:L703378:occurrences]

This Greek LXX noun means “devilish” or “devil,” referring to an evil adversary or accuser. It can identify a being presented as opposing or accusing others, while “devilish” describes the character associated with such opposition. The word occurs 22 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books represented here, with its greatest concentration in Job. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains an adversarial, evil figure or character.

This LXX Greek verb means to “make thoroughly manifest”—to bring something fully into the open or make it clearly known. As a verb, it describes the act of explaining, revealing, or making a matter unmistakable rather than merely mentioning it. It occurs 10 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek books represented here, including Deuteronomy, Daniel, and 1–2 Maccabees. Its exact force in any verse depends on what is being made clear in that passage.

This word means “beam,” referring to a substantial piece of wood used in construction or as part of a building. It is a noun describing structural timber, such as the wooden supports of a house or other structure. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs six times, all within six verses, and its ordinary sense remains concrete and practical rather than abstract. The surrounding verse determines the particular building or object in view.

This word means “5” and functions as an indeclinable number, identifying the quantity five. It is a numerical marker rather than a word describing a person, action, or spiritual quality. In the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), it occurs once, in Psalm 118:33. Its basic meaning is therefore precise and limited: it tells the reader that five items, persons, or units are being counted, while the surrounding verse determines what is being numbered.

This word means “I,” referring to the speaker or person presenting himself or herself in a sentence. It is a pronoun, so it identifies the person who speaks, acts, experiences something, or makes a statement. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 1,352 times, showing that it is a common way for a speaker to refer directly to himself or herself. Its exact emphasis in any passage depends on the surrounding words and context.

This adverb means “in all likelihood” or “suitably,” expressing that something is reasonably expected or appropriately done. It can describe a conclusion that makes good sense or an action that fits the circumstances. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 4 Maccabees 9:2. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic function is to qualify an action, judgment, or statement as fitting or probable.

This word means “each,” referring to members of a group one by one rather than only to the group as a whole. It is an adjective that points to individuals separately, whether people or things, and can stress that every member is considered in turn. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek books, it appears 328 times, showing that this is a common way to express individual members within a larger group.

This word describes someone or something that stands out from all others as distinguished or preeminent. It expresses exceptional distinction—the quality of being notably above or apart from the rest. As an adjective or noun, it can identify what is outstanding rather than merely ordinary. In the Greek Old Testament and Greek additions represented here, it occurs twice, once in 1 Kings and once in 3 Maccabees. Its precise emphasis in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and sentence.

This noun means “carrying out,” referring to the act or process of taking something out or bringing it forth. It names an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, all within two verses in 2 Chronicles. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and subject, but its central sense remains the carrying out of something.

This Greek LXX verb means “get by barter”: to obtain or conduct a transaction through exchange rather than ordinary purchase. It describes the act of trading goods or value with another person. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament, at Amos 8:5, so its broader range of use cannot be established from repeated biblical examples. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the basic idea is gaining something through bargaining or exchange.

This noun refers to dressing in—putting on clothing or covering oneself with something. It names the act or process of being clothed rather than a person, garment, or completed outfit. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in Esther and Job, so its basic meaning is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not provided here. Its precise force in either passage depends on the immediate context.

This Greek Old Testament verb means to arm oneself—to prepare with weapons for action or conflict. It describes becoming equipped and ready, whether referring to one person or a group. The word occurs nine times in the Greek Old Testament, especially in Numbers, and is also found in Deuteronomy and Joshua. Its use in passages about people going out together emphasizes readiness to act, not merely possessing equipment. The exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This word is a verb that expresses an action or state. Its basic sense is “six times”. It tells how many times something happens, marking a repeated action or event with the number six. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears three times, showing a precise numerical meaning rather than a broad description of repetition. Its use is found in Joshua, 2 Kings, and Job, though the surrounding verse text is needed to explain each particular setting.

This Greek LXX noun means “bringing in; supplying”—the act of introducing something or providing what is needed. It can describe provision or the arrival of something brought into a situation, while the surrounding sentence determines the precise sense. The word occurs 12 times in the Greek LXX corpus, appearing especially in Sirach, and also in Deuteronomy and Isaiah. Its basic idea remains active and practical: something is brought in or supplied rather than merely possessing or observing it.

This verb means “renew” or “revive”: to make something fresh, active, or strong again. It describes restoration rather than merely beginning something for the first time. In the Greek Old Testament, the Septuagint, this word occurs once, at Job 10:17. That single occurrence shows that its basic sense is focused and specific, while the surrounding verse is needed to explain exactly what is being renewed or revived there.

This verb means “look on”: it describes directing one’s gaze toward someone or something. It can simply identify the act of looking, without by itself stating the observer’s emotion, purpose, or judgment. In the LXX corpus, the word occurs 101 times, appearing throughout the Old Testament Greek books and related Greek writings included in that corpus. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This noun means “forgetfulness”: the failure to remember something or the state of no longer keeping it in mind. It names an absence or loss of memory rather than an action someone deliberately performs. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Sirach 11:27. The exact force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic meaning remains the loss or neglect of remembrance.

Eseban, also rendered Esevan, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a particular person in the Greek Old Testament. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 1 Chronicles 1:41. Without the surrounding verse text, its meaning is limited to the person’s name; the passage itself supplies any further significance.

gl: fineness of the day; good weather
d: fineness of the day; good weather

e.t: This noun refers to fine weather or a pleasant, favorable day. It describes good conditions in the day rather than a person, object, or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times, all in 2 Maccabees and 3 Maccabees. The word can therefore point to the goodness or pleasantness of the day’s conditions, with the surrounding sentence determining its precise use. Its central idea remains favorable weather or a fine day.

Euilat, also rendered Eilat, is a proper name used for a particular person or place in the Greek Old Testament. The name itself does not describe an action, quality, or spiritual idea; it identifies someone or somewhere named Euilat. It occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament, in Genesis, 1 Samuel, and 1 Chronicles. The surrounding verse is needed to determine whether each occurrence refers to a person or a location.

This word means “sun,” the bright heavenly body that gives daylight and marks the course of the day. It is a noun used throughout the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings, appearing 119 times in this Greek LXX corpus. Its ordinary meaning remains direct and concrete, though a particular passage may use the sun within a comparison or poetic image. The word occurs from Genesis through Song of Songs, showing its broad use for the visible sun in biblical language.

This Greek LXX noun means “door”: the opening or entrance that gives access to a room, building, tent, or enclosed place. It can refer to an actual doorway and may be rendered in the plural when more than one entrance is meant. The word occurs 202 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, showing that it is a normal term for a physical entrance throughout this corpus. Its precise significance in any particular passage comes from the surrounding verse and context.

Iachirani, also rendered Iakhirani, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a particular named entity in the Greek Old Testament text. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at Numbers 26:42. The available lexical information gives the name itself but does not specify beyond that what person, family, or group it identifies in the verse.

Iebatha, also rendered Ievatha, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a named person, place, or other entity in the Greek Old Testament tradition, though the available information does not specify which kind of entity it names. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at Joshua 21:25. Its exact referent is determined by the surrounding passage, not by the name itself.

Iemēr, also rendered Iemir, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Septuagint, it occurs once, in Nehemiah 7:61. The available lexical information identifies the name itself but does not provide its meaning as a common noun or explain the person’s identity. Its specific significance in that passage therefore comes from the surrounding list and context, not from the name alone.

Ieroboam is a proper name identifying a person, rather than a word describing an object, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs 105 times, appearing most often in 1 Kings, 2 Kings, and 2 Chronicles. The name is also found once in the deuterocanonical writings. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on which person named Ieroboam is being discussed, but the word itself functions as a personal name throughout these occurrences.

This is a proper name, given as “Indos” or “Inthos.” It identifies a named entity rather than describing an action, quality, or general object. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 6:37. The available lexical information does not specify from the name alone whether the named entity is a person or place, so its precise referent must come from the surrounding verse and passage.

This noun refers to “one enjoying equal political rights”—a person recognized as having the same political standing and civic rights as others. It describes equality in participation within a political community, not merely personal friendship or general fairness. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 3 Maccabees 2:30. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “follow after”: to go behind someone or come after them. It describes movement in which one person or group proceeds after another, rather than leading or going alongside. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, in Jeremiah, Daniel, and 1 Maccabees. Its exact force in any one verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains following after someone or something.

This verb means “saw up”: it describes cutting something with a saw, especially cutting it apart or into pieces. It is an action word, naming what someone does rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Susanna 1:59. The surrounding verse would determine exactly what is being sawn and how the action functions in that sentence.

This word means “nest.” It is a noun used to name a nest. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs three times: once each in 1 Chronicles, Ezekiel, and Wisdom. Its central meaning is simple and concrete; it refers to the nest itself rather than describing an action or person. The surrounding sentence determines how the word functions in each passage, since the verse text is needed to explain its specific use.

This noun refers to a mixture, especially a drink that has been prepared or poured out. It describes something blended or offered as a liquid rather than a person, action, or abstract idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs only twice, in Psalms 74:9 and Isaiah 65:11, so its normal meaning is focused and specific. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis falls on the mixture itself or on its being poured out.

This word means “dust” or “cloud of dust,” referring to fine particles lying on the ground or rising into the air. It is a noun used in the Greek Old Testament to describe a visible, earthly substance. The word occurs six times in the Greek Old Testament, appearing in Deuteronomy, Job, Isaiah, and Amos. Its basic meaning remains consistent across these uses: loose dust or a mass of dust. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis is on dust covering something, being formed, or being stirred up.

This word is a proper name, referring to a person or place named “Leb” or “Lev.” It functions as a name rather than describing an action, quality, or common object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Joshua 19:29. The name’s precise reference and significance depend on the surrounding verse and passage, since the lexical meaning itself identifies the name but does not describe the context in which it appears.

This word means “shell” or “husk,” referring to the outer covering that surrounds and protects what is inside. It is a noun used for a plant’s outer layer rather than for the inner substance itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Song of Songs. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the word’s precise poetic force in each occurrence must be understood from its immediate context. Its basic idea remains the exterior covering or thin outer part of something.

Lod, also rendered Loth, is a proper name used for a specific named entity rather than a general quality, action, or description. Its meaning is therefore chiefly identifying: it names Lod, with “Loth” given as another form of the same name. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, the name occurs three times, in 1 Chronicles, Ezra, and Nehemiah. The name itself does not supply a broader abstract meaning without the surrounding verse.

This word means “cook,” a person whose work is preparing food. It is a noun, so it identifies the person rather than the cooking action itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, and each recorded rendering is “cook.” The word appears twice in 1 Samuel 9 and once in Lamentations 2, showing its ordinary, practical use for someone responsible for preparing food. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Masek is a proper name, rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. Its meaning is simply the name “Masek.” In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at Genesis 15:2. Because it is a personal or place name in the text, its significance comes from the surrounding passage and the person or location it identifies, not from a broader everyday definition.

This Greek LXX verb means to defraud someone or deal deceitfully with them. It describes dishonest action toward another person rather than merely making a mistake or acting unwisely. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Samuel 19:28, so its broader range of use cannot be established from repeated passages. Its basic sense remains clear: treating someone dishonestly for wrongful advantage. The precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the wording being described.

This Greek LXX verb means “fetch”: to go and bring someone or something to the speaker or another person. It describes an action of obtaining or bringing, rather than merely seeing or calling. The word appears five times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, including Genesis, Numbers, 2 Maccabees, and 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on who is being fetched and why, but its central idea remains the act of bringing someone or something as requested.

This adverb expresses concern about something unwanted happening, meaning “lest somehow” or “in case somehow.” It introduces a possibility that someone wants to avoid or guard against. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in Sirach 28:26. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its ordinary function is to warn of a possible undesirable outcome rather than to state that the outcome has happened.

This noun refers to something “with but one horn.” It describes a horned creature or figure by emphasizing that it has a single horn. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs eight times across eight verses, appearing in Numbers, Deuteronomy, Job, and Psalms. Its basic meaning is descriptive rather than abstract: it identifies a being through this distinctive physical feature. The surrounding verse determines whether the word is being used in a literal description or in imagery, but the word itself centers on the idea of one horn.

This proper noun refers to an Odollamite, also rendered Othollamitis. It is a personal or identifying name associated with Odollam in the Greek Old Testament wording. The word occurs three times, all in Genesis 38, so its normal function is to identify a person connected with that name rather than describe an action, quality, or abstract idea. Its precise significance in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This verb means to “wail aloud” or “lament,” describing a spoken or cried-out expression of grief or distress. It is an action word: it tells what someone does when expressing deep sorrow aloud. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 12:14. The word’s basic meaning is clear from its definition, while the surrounding verse would be needed to explain the particular situation in which the lament occurs.

This Greek LXX noun means “downpour,” referring to a heavy fall of rain. It names rain as a forceful, abundant event rather than merely a light shower. The word occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this corpus, appearing in Deuteronomy, Daniel, Wisdom, and Sirach. Its precise force in any individual passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central meaning remains a powerful or abundant rainfall. [p03:word:lxx:L709611:identity] [p03:word:lxx:L709611:occurrences]

Oukan is a proper name, referring to a person named “Oukan” or “Ukan.” The name appears once in the Greek LXX, in Genesis 36:27. Because the available information identifies the name but does not include the verse’s wording or surrounding passage, its personal significance and role in that genealogy cannot be described further here. The two forms, “Oukan” and “Ukan,” represent the same named individual in this word entry.

This Greek LXX verb means to “shut out” or “exclude”—to prevent someone or something from entering, joining, or being included. It describes an action rather than a person or object. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical corpus, in 2 Maccabees 4:34. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and its subject, but the central idea remains deliberate exclusion or keeping something outside.

This noun means “open sea,” referring to the broad expanse of salt water rather than a small shore or enclosed body of water. It presents the sea as a wide, unobstructed space. In the Greek Old Testament tradition represented here, it occurs twice, once in 2 Maccabees and once in 4 Maccabees. The exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and its description, but the word itself carries the straightforward sense of the open sea.

This word means “breadth,” referring to how wide or broad something is. As a noun, it describes a measurable dimension, especially when giving the size of a structure, object, or area. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it is used 50 times, often in descriptions of buildings, rooms, land, or other physical spaces. Its basic idea is the side-to-side extent of something, complementing measurements such as length or height. The surrounding passage determines exactly what is being measured, but the word itself points to width or breadth.

This word means “flock,” referring to a group of animals kept or gathered together, especially sheep. It is a noun used for an actual herd rather than for one individual animal. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 70 times, appearing across passages that mention flocks as possessions, sources of food, or animals being tended and counted. Its basic meaning remains consistent wherever it appears, while the surrounding verse identifies the particular flock or situation being described.

This word means “gentleness,” describing a mild, considerate quality rather than harshness or force. As a noun, it names this quality itself. In the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), it occurs once, in Sirach 1:27, so its wider range of use within that corpus cannot be established from repeated examples. The word’s central idea remains a quiet, gracious manner that treats others with care. The precise emphasis in Sirach 1:27 depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This noun refers to a porch or portico: a covered entrance or passage connected with a building. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Judges 3:22. The word identifies a physical architectural space rather than an action, person, or abstract idea. Its precise significance in that occurrence depends on the surrounding verse and passage, since the verse text is not included here. The central meaning remains a porch or portico, understood as part of a building’s structure.

Raa (also rendered “Rhaa”) is a proper name, referring to a named place rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Joshua 15:33, and is rendered “Raa.” Because it is a place name, its meaning is its identifying role: it designates that location in the biblical record, not a general concept.

Remoth, also rendered Rhimoth, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Ezra 10:29. The available lexical information preserves the name itself but does not identify whether Remoth refers to a person, place, or another named entity. Its precise referent therefore belongs to the surrounding passage, while its basic meaning is the proper name “Rēmōth; Rhimoth.”

This noun appears to mean “ranks?”—ordered lines or groups, though the question mark indicates that the precise sense is uncertain. It occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, both times in 2 Kings 11. Its basic role is to refer to an arrangement of people or units standing or organized in order. The surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly what kind of ranks are intended in each occurrence.

Salpaad is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament translation, referring to a person named Salpaad, also rendered Salpaath. It appears twelve times in the LXX across nine verses, with most occurrences in Numbers and additional occurrences in Joshua and 1 Chronicles. The name itself does not describe a quality, action, or teaching; it serves to identify this person.

“Saphthaibaithme” is a proper name preserved in the Greek Old Testament, also appearing as “Safthevethme.” It does not describe an action, quality, or general idea; it identifies a particular named entity. This word occurs once in the Greek LXX, in Joshua 19:27. Since the surrounding verse text is not included here, its precise identification in that passage cannot be explained further, but its lexical function is clear: it is a name rather than a common descriptive word.

Sebocha is a proper name, referring to a person rather than expressing a general quality, action, or object. It is rendered as “Sebocha” and is also represented as “Sevokha,” preserving the name in English rather than translating it into an ordinary descriptive word. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, at 2 Samuel 21:18. The name’s specific significance in that passage must be understood from the surrounding verse and passage, since the word itself functions chiefly as a personal designation.

Semai, also rendered Seme, is a proper name referring to a person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 4:17. Because it is a personal name rather than a descriptive word, its meaning is chiefly identifying: it distinguishes this individual from others in the genealogy. The English forms “Semai” and “Seme” represent the same named person in this LXX occurrence.

This LXX Greek verb means “scatter”: to spread people or things apart rather than keep them together. It describes an action that causes separation or dispersal. The word occurs 15 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books represented here, so its basic sense is used across several kinds of passages. As a verb, it expresses what someone does—scattering people, objects, or other things. The precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This noun means “head of grain,” the clustered top portion of a cereal plant where the grains develop. It refers to the part of a growing crop that can be full, thin, healthy, or damaged, depending on the condition of the plant. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 19 times across 15 verses, especially in descriptions of grain and agricultural produce. Its precise significance in any particular passage comes from the surrounding context, but its ordinary meaning remains the grain-bearing head of a plant.

This word means “love” or “affection,” expressing a warm bond of care and attachment. It is a noun, so it names this kind of loving feeling rather than describing an action. In the Greek Old Testament-related writings represented here, it occurs four times: once in 3 Maccabees and three times in 4 Maccabees. Its English renderings include “affection” and “love,” which reflect the same central idea. The precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself points to personal, heartfelt attachment.

e.h: Pierce Together or Stab at Once
e.t: This Greek LXX verb means “pierce together; stab at once.” It describes a forceful piercing or stabbing action carried out simultaneously or in one decisive movement. The word occurs twice in the LXX corpus, both in 2 Maccabees: 12:23 and 13:15. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and scene, but its central idea is direct, coordinated stabbing or piercing rather than a general touch or strike.

Syros, also written Siros, is a proper name used for a person or place identified by that name in the Greek Old Testament. It is not a general word describing an action, quality, or object, so its precise referent must be determined from the surrounding passage. This name occurs 28 times in the Greek Old Testament, across 25 verses, from Genesis through Amos. The name appears especially often in 1 Chronicles and Genesis. Its meaning is therefore its identifying name, rather than a broader concept or idea.

This Greek LXX noun refers to something intended “for breeding.” It describes a breeding purpose rather than a general activity or quality. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at 1 Kings 2:46. Because no verse text is included here, its precise role in that sentence must be understood from the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains focused on breeding use or purpose.

This adjective describes something worked or shaped by a wheel. It points to the manner in which an object has been made, emphasizing wheel-based work rather than naming the object itself. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, the word occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 11:10. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its established meaning remains “worked by a wheel.”

This adjective describes someone as “wanton” or “insolent”—unrestrained, offensively bold, or disrespectful in conduct. It characterizes a person by a shameless or domineering manner rather than naming a specific action. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs only twice: once in Proverbs and once in Sirach. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is arrogant disregard for proper restraint or respect.

This verb means “melt exceedingly,” describing something undergoing an intense or complete melting. As a verb, it expresses an action or process rather than naming a person, object, or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 7:12. The word’s exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense remains the idea of melting to an extreme degree.

This noun means “at the breast,” describing a nursing infant or one still being fed at the breast. It presents the person as dependent on a mother for nourishment rather than able to feed independently. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, in Hosea 14:1. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning points to the condition of being at the breast.

gl: play a role; act in pretence
d: play a role; act in pretence

e.t: This Greek LXX verb means “play a role” or “act in pretence.” It describes behaving as though one is someone or something else, presenting an appearance rather than acting plainly and sincerely. As a verb, it expresses this kind of performed behavior. It occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Sirach 4:30; the surrounding verse text is needed to explain its precise force there.

This adjective describes someone who loves honor or is covetous of honor. It points to a strong desire for esteem or recognition, rather than simply identifying a person who receives honor. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs twice, in Wisdom and 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its central meaning remains a person or attitude marked by a desire for honor.

This Greek LXX verb means “mix”: to combine things so that they are blended together. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at 2 Samuel 20:12; its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its basic sense remains the act of mixing or blending, whether referring to materials or things brought together.

This adjective means “luminous,” describing something that gives off light or appears bright. It points to visible brightness rather than naming a person, place, or action. In the Greek Old Testament material represented here, it occurs twice, both times in Sirach. The surrounding verse text is needed to determine exactly what is described in each occurrence, but the word’s basic sense remains something radiant, light-giving, or shining. It should therefore be understood as a descriptive word for brightness within its particular sentence.

Chermel, also rendered Khermel, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a named person or place in the Greek Old Testament tradition, but the available material does not specify which in each occurrence. The name appears six times across four verses, in Joshua and Isaiah. Its exact reference depends on the surrounding verse, yet its basic function remains that of a name: it identifies a particular named entity rather than expressing a general idea.
